summary:
Flames of Aron is an agent-based hybrid RAG system that answers questions about NASA's microgravity combustion experiments. It indexes 95 sources from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive: 1,638 text chunks plus structured tables with 536 test rows from FLEX, BASS, BASS-II and Saffire. These are linked into evidence records, rules and 66 flagged conflicts between sources.

Each question goes through an agent pipeline. The system classifies the question, searches text and tables together, calls tools (such as a PSI test query and a lunar-atmosphere check), and an LLM writes the answer. A validator checks it against the evidence and retries once. Every answer carries citations, and questions the data cannot support are refused instead of invented. On our training evaluation, answer-type accuracy was 1.0 and 8 of 8 unanswerable questions were correctly refused.

Example finding: none of the 273 known tests matches lunar-habitat conditions (O2 >= 30%, pressure <= 10.2 psi). The closest, FLEX #37, ran at 34% O2 and 10.33 psi, a gap for future fire-safety testing.

The Streamlit web app lets anyone ask questions, browse experiments and inspect evidence. Users can add their own free Gemini, Groq or Mistral API key (kept only in session memory); without one, the app shows an evidence summary. Chat history is private per visitor.
Our Projects Github Repository Link: https://github.com/SE-220717006/Flames_of_Aron
details:
What it does: Flames of Aron lets anyone ask plain-language questions about NASA's microgravity combustion experiments and get cited, verifiable answers. Researchers and students normally have to dig through dozens of PDFs, data tables and papers to learn, for example, how flame spread changes with oxygen level, pressure or flow speed. Our system does that search for them. It indexes 95 sources from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive: 1,638 text chunks, structured tables with 536 test rows (FLEX, BASS, BASS-II, Saffire), 393 evidence records, 25 facts, 8 rules and 66 flagged conflicts between sources.

How it works: Each question goes through an agent pipeline. The agent classifies the question, searches text and structured tables together, and calls tools such as a PSI test query and a lunar-atmosphere check. An LLM then writes the answer from the retrieved evidence only. A validator checks the answer against that evidence and retries once if needed. Every claim carries a citation. If the data cannot support a question, the system refuses instead of inventing an answer.

Benefits and impact: Faster, trustworthy access to hard-to-search spaceflight fire-safety knowledge. Because conflicts between sources are shown rather than hidden, users see where the evidence disagrees. Example: none of the 273 known tests matches lunar-habitat conditions (O2 >= 30%, pressure <= 10.2 psi); the closest, FLEX #37 (34% O2, 10.33 psi), shows a gap for future testing. The intended impact is to help engineers, students and mission planners find such gaps quickly.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, Plotly, sentence-transformers for embeddings, Gemini / Groq / Mistral LLM APIs, pytest (102 passing tests), GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud. No special hardware is needed.

Creativity: Retrieval is combined with data tools and an explicit refusal policy, so it behaves like a careful analyst rather than a chatbot. It also works without an LLM: with no API key it shows an evidence summary.

Factors we considered: Hallucination risk (validator, citations, refusals); free public access for judges (users add their own free API key, kept only in session memory and never saved); privacy (chat history is private per visitor); and honest limits (ACME CFI-G tables are not yet in the lunar screen).
